## 1. The wind with frost in it  (`#the-wind-and-the-tilth`)

Cited ayat: 3:117

> **3:117** مَثَلُ مَا يُنفِقُونَ فِى هَٰذِهِ ٱلْحَيَوٰةِ ٱلدُّنْيَا كَمَثَلِ رِيحٍ فِيهَا صِرٌّ أَصَابَتْ حَرْثَ قَوْمٍ ظَلَمُوٓا۟ أَنفُسَهُمْ فَأَهْلَكَتْهُ وَمَا ظَلَمَهُمُ ٱللَّهُ وَلَٰكِنْ أَنفُسَهُمْ يَظْلِمُونَ

### Claims

**c1** (3:117): The ayah says that the similitude of what they spend in the life of this world is like a wind with sirr in it that struck the tilth of a people who wronged themselves and destroyed it.

**c2** (3:117): God did not wrong them, but they wrong themselves.

### One-minute summary

The ayah likens what they spend in the life of this world to a wind with sirr in it that destroyed the tilth of a people who wronged themselves [c1]. It adds that God did not wrong them, but they wrong themselves [c2].

### Complete story

The ayah says that the similitude of what they spend in the life of this world is like a wind with sirr in it [c1]. The wind struck the tilth of a people who wronged themselves and destroyed it [c1]. God did not wrong them, but they wrong themselves [c2].

### Deep study

The ayah gives the similitude and then states who did the wrong: God did not wrong them, and they wrong themselves [c1][c2]. The Arabic word sirr is read as a biting frost or as a loud sound, and this draft leaves it open [c1].

### Kids mode

The ayah likens what they spend in the life of this world to a wind that destroyed the tilth of a people who wronged themselves [c1]. God did not wrong them [c2].

### Life lessons (educational interpretation)

Educational interpretation (not scripture): One reading is that the ayah shows spending that does not last, like tilth that the wind destroys [c1]. Another reading is that the ayah places the wrong with the people themselves, not with God [c2].

### What the sources do not establish

- Not established: who they are in this ayah; the pronoun points to people described in ayat before 3:117, which are outside the ayat cited for this item.
- Not established: where or when the tilth was struck, or whose it was; the people are not named.
- The word sirr is read as a biting frost or a loud sound; this draft leaves it open.
- The ayah itself uses the word for a similitude (mathal).
